summary: Make every screen transition as fast as you can without removing it, and when a transition has to cover loading, make it fit your game instead of leaving players on a slow fade and a black screen.
takeaways: Making players wait is a sin; transitions are rarely too fast
Keep a brief transition; removing it entirely feels jarring
Hide loading with transitions that fit and add mood
Use themed wipes instead of plain fades

principles.principle: Make screen transitions fast, but don't remove them entirely
principles.why: Making players wait is a sin: slow fades and long black screens leave players without control and rob them of their time. It's almost impossible to be too fast, though cutting transitions entirely feels jarring.
principles.how: Time every fade and black screen and trim each to a hasty speed that still reads as a transition.
principles.anti_pattern: Slow, dreary fadeouts followed by lengthy black screens.
principles.example: Smash Bros. Ultimate uses random wipes to transition to the victory screen.
principles.quote: A hasty speed is just right!

principles.principle: Disguise loading behind transitions that fit the game and add mood
principles.why: Many games use transitions to cover loading even without a loading icon, and done well they add to the experience, as Resident Evil's doors masked loading while creating fear.
principles.how: Turn the loading cover into an in-world event (a door, a key) or a wipe that matches your theme, kept at an acceptable speed.
principles.example: Original Resident Evil doors, which took longer to open when zombies were on the other side; Super Mario World's key transition adding mystery.
principles.quote: There's always a way to make these things fit with your game.

principles.principle: Scroll between fixed-camera screens so players see how the map connects
principles.why: The first Zelda's edge-of-screen scrolling made a fixed camera easier to play with and showed how screens fit together, though today it could be smoother and faster.
principles.how: Use a quick, smooth scroll for screen-to-screen movement instead of a cut or fade, and keep it from wasting time.
principles.example: The Legend of Zelda (first game) edge scrolling.
principles.quote: It's fundamental to both do what's right for your game, and make sure you're not wasting the player's time.

summary: When you balance characters or moves, keep their peaks and valleys and nerf a secondary parameter instead of averaging everything out, because options that feel alike make the whole game bland.
takeaways: Shaving strengths and filling weaknesses makes fighters feel the same
Keep peaks and valleys; variety is the game's lifeblood
Nerf a secondary parameter, keep the defining strength
Divisive options are good: let players settle it in matches

principles.principle: Keep each option's peaks and valleys instead of averaging them out
principles.why: The more alike fighters' abilities become, the more they feel like the same character, which gives the whole game a bland feel; variety is what keeps it fresh.
principles.how: When something is too strong, don't also soften its weaknesses; keep a distinct strength and weakness for every option, in competitive and non-competitive games alike.
principles.anti_pattern: Shaving down a strength while lessening the weaknesses to compensate.
principles.example: Smash Bros. fighter balancing, driven by the Balancing Team's daily matches and online match data.
principles.quote: Variety among things like fighters is the very lifeblood of the game!

principles.principle: Nerf a secondary parameter and leave the move's defining strength intact
principles.why: One attack has many components (power, speed, duration, windup, follow-through, range, hit size, animation speed, knockback, combo ability, shield damage, shield recovery), so it can be weakened without erasing its character.
principles.how: Keep the characteristic attack power but lengthen the vulnerable follow-through, or shrink the hitbox.
principles.anti_pattern: Flattening the stat that makes the move distinctive.
principles.example: Smash Bros. move adjustments.
principles.quote: leave the move's characteristic attack power untouched, and instead lengthen the follow-through— a time when the fighter is vulnerable.

principles.principle: Embrace divisive options that make players want to settle it in a match
principles.why: If one player says A is better and another says B is better, the differences are fueling play; balance that isn't divisive would be the real problem. Social media echo chambers make this harder, but creators can't shy away.
principles.how: Push the dynamic range between options as far as possible instead of sanding down whatever splits opinion.
principles.anti_pattern: Backing away from distinctive designs because biases spread quickly on social media.
principles.quote: You want those players to say: "Then let's settle it in a match!"

summary: If you can get permission, have elementary school children play your game in a relaxed, fun setting and quietly watch them, because their honest reactions expose control problems and boredom that adults hide.
takeaways: Children give honest reactions to controls and boredom
Watch kids play rather than asking them questions
Make sessions feel like fun with friends, with snacks
Get permission first; confidentiality and child welfare matter

principles.principle: Watch children play your build instead of asking them questions
principles.why: Children, unlike jaded adults, always react honestly, revealing difficulties with the controls and what bores them.
principles.how: With permission, invite staff members' kids and their friends, stand back, and note where they struggle or lose interest.
principles.anti_pattern: Asking them directly what they think.
principles.example: A child playing the original Smash Bros. shouted at how far a Falcon Punch knocked someone back.
principles.quote: Rather than asking them directly, I would stand back and just try and see how they responded to the game.

principles.principle: Make playtests feel like a fun session with friends
principles.why: Snacks and friends make it feel less like play testing and more like a fun gaming session, so reactions stay natural.
principles.how: Let kids come in groups, provide snacks and keep the setting casual, after getting the permissions confidentiality and child well-being require.
principles.quote: We'd prepare things like snacks, too, to help it to feel less like actual play testing and more like a fun gaming session with friends.

principles.principle: Use outside playtest reactions to keep the dev team motivated
principles.why: The team was always happy to have these sessions, and during especially tough work they drive you forward.
principles.how: Schedule kid playtests during hard stretches and let the team see or hear the reactions.
principles.quote: When you're pushing through some especially tough work, stuff like this can really drive you forward.

summary: Treat every coworker as someone you'll work with again: never fight, badmouth people or leave on bad terms, because the game industry is small and that behavior comes back to you.
takeaways: The game industry is small; colleagues reappear years later
Never fight, badmouth, or leave on bad terms
Give constructive feedback openly; distance yourself if needed
Focus on supportive teammates, not unpleasant ones

principles.principle: Never fight with or badmouth coworkers; you will meet them again
principles.why: Developers move between teams constantly and the industry is small, so someone you wronged may join your next team years later; treating people poorly gets you excluded.
principles.how: Leave every team on good terms, finish or hand off your work instead of abandoning a project, and don't speak ill of anyone.
principles.anti_pattern: Fighting, acting selfishly, leaving on bad terms, or abandoning a project to dive into the next job.
principles.example: Directors at other companies ask Sakurai about former team members who are interviewing with them.
principles.quote: Unfortunately, the game industry is much smaller than you might think. So, never get into fights!

principles.principle: Raise problems as constructive feedback, then step back rather than resent
principles.why: Speaking your mind often benefits everyone and distancing yourself from a bad fit is fine, but disliking people comes straight back to you.
principles.how: Bring issues up directly and constructively; if a situation still doesn't suit you, distance yourself instead of escalating or holding a grudge.
principles.anti_pattern: Thinking poorly of people.
principles.quote: It's okay to distance yourself from a situation that doesn't suit you. And it's okay to be up-front with constructive feedback.

principles.principle: Put your attention on supportive teammates, not the unpleasant few
principles.why: You're responsible for your workplace's atmosphere, and fixating on difficult people draws attention away from the supportive ones who cause no issues.
principles.how: Engage with the people who help, and keep the team aimed at one common goal.
principles.quote: teams and coworkers should be striving together toward a single, common goal.

summary: Treat play time as a cost the player pays, not a selling point: build the fun first, let long play time follow from it, and keep the player in control for as much of that time as possible.
takeaways: Advertised play time feels like a cost, not a perk
Games compete with everything else for players' time
Build fun first; let play time follow
Maximize the time players spend in control

principles.principle: Treat play time as a cost to the player, not a selling point
principles.why: Hearing a game takes hundreds of hours can make people pass on it, because they weigh that time against everything else they could be doing.
principles.how: Don't lead marketing or design with hour counts; present the fun and let length be a by-product.
principles.anti_pattern: Selling the game with "This game has 300 hours of content!"
principles.quote: Play time—especially how it's perceived before starting a game— is better thought of as a cost, of sorts.

principles.principle: Build fun first and let play time fall into place later
principles.why: Time spent on a game should be a result of how fun it is, as when players spend hundreds or thousands of hours in Smash Bros.
principles.how: Prioritize fun experiences and the systems that reinforce that fun before deciding how much content to make.
principles.anti_pattern: Padding length to hit an hour target.
principles.example: Smash Bros., which some people have played for hundreds or thousands of hours.
principles.quote: Still, the time you spend on a game should be a result of how fun that game is!

principles.principle: Maximize the share of time the player is in control
principles.why: Sakurai always watches how much time the player spends in control, because the longer they're in control, the better.
principles.how: Measure non-interactive time in a session (cutscenes, loading, menus, transitions) and cut it.
principles.quote: That's because the longer they're in control of the game, the better.

principles.principle: Give your game enough appeal to beat low-effort phone content
principles.why: Phones and social media offer diverse content with a low barrier to entry, while games take more effort to get started.
principles.how: Make sure the game's appeal is clear and strong enough to justify the effort of starting it.
principles.example: People's free time going to phones and tablets.
principles.quote: Games have a comparatively higher barrier to entry and take more effort to get started, so it'll be difficult if your game doesn't have the appeal to overcome that.

summary: When you animate anything that isn't a machine, never rotate on a single axis: pair the main turn with a second axis, move the connected joints, and hand-tune the timing so the motion looks believable and has personality.
takeaways: Single-axis rotation looks mechanical; combine two axes
Move shoulder and collarbone with a twisting wrist
Hand-tune curves: offset axes, add counter-motion
Plan head turns together with eye movement

principles.principle: Rotate organic motion on two axes, never just one
principles.why: A head turned only around the Y axis feels mechanical and a one-axis wrist twist looks like a drill; tilting a bit before turning is more believable.
principles.how: Layer a dip (X axis) or tilt (Z axis) onto every Y-axis turn of heads, wrists and torsos.
principles.anti_pattern: Pure single-axis rotation on characters.
principles.example: Sakurai's own head turn, shown first on one axis.
principles.quote: When creating human movement, make it a point to rotate on two axes.

principles.principle: Move connected joints along with the rotating part
principles.why: Connected parts move in reality: the shoulder and collarbone work in tandem with the wrist.
principles.how: When animating a twist such as revving a motorcycle, shift the shoulder and collarbone along with the wrist.
principles.example: Revving a motorcycle.
principles.quote: The shoulder and collarbone work in tandem with the wrist, for example.

principles.principle: Hand-tune rotation timing instead of trusting software curves
principles.why: Generated function curves can look believable, but how a rotation reaches its end pose decides its personality.
principles.how: Slightly offset the timing of the two axes, add an occasional counter-motion, and choose a downward, upward or level path on purpose.
principles.anti_pattern: Accepting the 3D software's default function curves as-is.
principles.quote: even rotations that finish in the same place can express drastically different personalities depending on how they reach that point.

principles.principle: Account for the eye line before finalizing head turns
principles.why: Animators often turn the whole head fully before facial animation exists, and once the eyes are added the turn can be bigger than wanted.
principles.how: Plan eye direction with the head turn, and reduce the head rotation once the eyes carry part of the look.
principles.anti_pattern: Over-turning the head before the eyes are animated.
principles.quote: once the eye line gets added in, that large of a head turn might just end up being a bigger movement than you want.

summary: Games are built for the screens they're shown on, and older games were made for CRTs (fast response, bright phosphors, light-gun timing, interlacing and hidden screen edges), so account for that hardware when you study, port or imitate them.
takeaways: Retro games were designed solely for CRT displays
CRTs respond fast; score-chasers still seek them out
Light guns relied on CRT scanline timing
Only about 490 of 525 scanlines were usable

principles.principle: Judge and design visuals for the display players actually use
principles.why: Games of the past were made solely with CRTs in mind, so their art, such as checkered pixel patterns, takes on a completely different texture on modern screens.
principles.how: When porting, remaking or imitating retro art, check dithering and brightness on the target display, and study originals the way they were meant to be seen.
principles.example: Checkered pixel patterns that look completely different on a CRT.
principles.quote: games of the past were made solely with these CRTs in mind— causing things to feel different in certain ways than they do nowadays.

principles.principle: Treat display response time as part of how the game feels
principles.why: CRTs need no buffer or image processor, so they respond fast, and score-chasers for classic games go out of their way to use them.
principles.how: Test timing-critical play on the displays your players use, knowing skilled players notice the difference in response.
principles.example: Score-chasers playing classic games on CRTs.
principles.quote: As opposed to LCD monitors, CRTs don't require a buffer or image processor, giving them fast response time.

principles.principle: Keep essential information inside the visible safe area
principles.why: On CRTs only about 490 of 525 scanlines were usable and the whole image was never visible, so developers assumed the edges would never be seen.
principles.how: On any display that may crop the image, leave margins at the edges and keep important elements out of them.
principles.example: NES-era games, where scrambled characters at the screen edge weren't a problem because no one saw them.
principles.quote: On a CRT display, you can't see the entire screen.

summary: Quality comes from relentless, specific polish passes, so check poses, follow-through, effect readability, contrast and both versions of every move, and flag even tiny flaws with visual paintovers as soon as you see them.
takeaways: Check special moves in both ground and aerial versions
Bright-only effects vanish on bright stages; mix in dark
Foreground contrast strong, background contrast weak
Give feedback with paintovers; flag tiny flaws immediately
Polishing without fail is what raises quality

principles.principle: Check every special move in both its ground and aerial versions
principles.why: Sora's Sonic Blade had drastically different aerial and ground poses, and its distance shrank when attacking upward, a type of bug.
principles.how: Play both versions of every special side by side, comparing poses and reach in each direction.
principles.example: Smash Ultimate, Sora's Sonic Blade.
principles.quote: For special moves, you need to check both the ground and aerial versions.

principles.principle: Mix dark elements into bright effects so they read on any stage
principles.why: Effects with only bright elements are hard to see on bright stages, and layered effects or heavy background atmosphere can bury the fighters.
principles.how: Add dark elements or smoke to bright effects, and cut back background atmosphere that conflicts with the visual effects.
principles.anti_pattern: Layered effects that make the fighters hard to see.
principles.example: Sora's Blizzaga; the Final Smash background's atmosphere cut back and extra smoke added to the explosion.
principles.quote: Effects with only bright elements are difficult to see on bright stages, so I asked for more dark elements to be mixed in.

principles.principle: Give the same material strong foreground contrast and weaker background contrast
principles.why: Reversed contrast, overly dark character lighting and platforms that blend in are common problems that hurt readability.
principles.how: On each stage, compare foreground and background contrast for the same material, and check that fighters, platforms and projectiles stand out without the floor overpowering them.
principles.anti_pattern: Contrast that's stronger in the background than the foreground.
principles.example: Hollow Bastion: fighters blending into stained glass, hard-to-see drop-through platforms, Greninja's Water Shuriken lost against the floor.
principles.quote: The same material should have strong contrast in the foreground, and weaker contrast in the background

principles.principle: Give visual feedback and point out tiny flaws immediately
principles.why: Small flaws are easy to overlook, and fine-tuning over and over is what raises quality.
principles.how: Send retouched images, quick mouse sketches or a posed figure instead of words alone, and flag stray marks the moment you see them.
principles.anti_pattern: Letting small flaws slide.
principles.example: Sora's forward aerial posed with a figure; an extraneous mark on the Timeless River costume's face.
principles.quote: These things are easy to overlook, so you should point them out as soon as you find them.

summary: Design your HUD to be both easy and fun to use, keeping useful information on screen while finding tricks so it doesn't crowd the play area.
takeaways: HUDs are useful but crowd the screen; balance both
Auto-hide cursors by distance and situation
Make HUD semi-transparent when characters overlap it
Use HUD portraits and motion to add character appeal
Make meters react to game state

principles.principle: Auto-hide or fade HUD elements that would obstruct play
principles.why: A HUD is useful but can crowd the screen, and player cursors would be an eyesore if always visible.
principles.how: Hide cursors based on distance and situation, and make HUD panels semi-transparent when a character overlaps them.
principles.anti_pattern: Always-visible markers cluttering the play area.
principles.example: Smash Bros. player cursors and semi-transparent HUD.
principles.quote: These would be a real eyesore if they were always visible, so they're made to automatically hide themselves based on distance and situation.

principles.principle: Use the HUD to add character appeal and energy
principles.why: Fighters are sometimes small on screen, so faces turned toward the audience boost appeal, and upward-scrolling patterns suggest burning spirit.
principles.how: Put character portraits facing the player in the HUD, and animate their backgrounds with UV scrolling rather than a flat, static image.
principles.example: Smash Bros. HUD from Brawl onward.
principles.quote: The fighters are sometimes quite small on-screen— so this helps boost their character appeal.

principles.principle: Make HUD elements react to game state and surface hard-to-track info
principles.why: In 3D it's hard to know how many opponents you've damaged, and meters that change or break make the HUD informative and fun to look at.
principles.how: Swap meters per ability, break them when the vehicle is destroyed, and show icons for opponents you've hit or defeated.
principles.example: Kirby Air Ride's ability meters and opponent icons; Meteos' alien head spinning faster with the Speeder.
principles.quote: In a 3D space, it can be difficult to know how many opponents you've dealt damage to, but I'd say this is an effective solution.

summary: Don't settle for perfectly straight motion or rotation around an exact center: add a wobble to trajectories and move pivots off-center so objects move with personality instead of following your software's bland defaults.
takeaways: Straight lines and center-point spins look mechanical
Add a looping positional wobble to projectiles
Offset rotation axes from the object's center
Don't just follow your software's tendencies

principles.principle: Add a looping wobble to straight-flying projectiles
principles.why: A cannonball flying in a straight line isn't interesting to look at; sliding the sprite around in a loop makes the shot feel completely different.
principles.how: Layer a six-frame positional loop (up, right-up, right-down, down, left-down, left-up) onto the projectile's path.
principles.example: Kirby's Shotzo and its "wobbly cannonballs," which also suited the Game Boy screen's afterimages.
principles.quote: If we simply sent the cannonballs flying forward in a straight line, it wouldn't be too interesting to look at.

principles.principle: Offset rotation axes slightly from the object's center
principles.why: Rotating around the exact center feels less organic, while a slightly shifted axis makes the motion a little erratic and expressive.
principles.how: Move the pivot of spinning items and swung weapons off the geometric center or grip, and compare it with the centered version.
principles.example: Smash Ultimate's bomb throw; Pyra's Blazing End, whose axis was moved off the sword's grip.
principles.quote: But the axis of rotation is shifted slightly away from the center of the bomb. It makes the movement feel a little erratic.

principles.principle: Don't let software defaults decide how things move
principles.why: Designers are used to straight lines and smooth circles, but animation means putting a soul into something unmoving, and defaults look bland.
principles.how: Review linear moves and center-point rotations in your game and give each some personality, using quick mock-ups during reviews.
principles.anti_pattern: Straight lines and smooth circles left as the software makes them.
principles.quote: try to find ways to avoid the blandness that can come from simply following your software's tendencies.

summary: Developers know their game too well to be the difficulty standard, so tune difficulty while handicapping yourself (one hand, less health, stricter conditions) and then make it easier than you think it should be.
takeaways: Developers know the game too well to set difficulty
Balancing to the best staff player locks buyers out
Handicap yourself: one hand, lower health, stricter rules
Make it easier than you think it should be

principles.principle: Don't use the dev team's skill as the difficulty standard
principles.why: Team members know the game inside out, so tuning to the best player, or even the median one, leaves it too hard for players who won't spend all their time on your game.
principles.how: Set difficulty a good deal below what feels right to the team, then make it easier still.
principles.anti_pattern: Balancing around the most skilled player on staff.
principles.quote: developers who already know a game shouldn't be considered as the standard— instead, make the game even easier than you think it should be, and it'll be just right.

principles.principle: Handicap yourself while tuning difficulty
principles.why: Playing one-handed makes even someone who knows the game well slip up, which brings the developer closer to a typical player.
principles.how: Test with one hand on the controller, reduced health, or stricter conditions, and tune so you can still clear it.
principles.example: Sakurai plays with one hand when balancing.
principles.quote: Playing the game with one hand, for example. It's easy to mess up even if I know the game well, so this is certainly an effective method.

principles.principle: Use fresh testers from the start, and each one only once
principles.why: Unfamiliar players are the best gauge, but they often lack time to finish and grow familiar, so the same person can't be called back a second or third time.
principles.how: Rotate in new testers who start from the very beginning, treating each as a one-time first impression.
principles.anti_pattern: Reusing the same outside tester as if they were still fresh.
principles.quote: Naturally, the best solution is to ask someone who's unfamiliar with your game to come play it from the start

summary: Treat music and sound effects as essential rather than secondary, because audio is what players remember first and what hits them in the heart, and no masterpiece has bad audio.
takeaways: No masterpiece has bad audio
Music and SFX are often what players remember first
Even simple noise effects can be well constructed
Good audio boosts enjoyment when players can listen

principles.principle: Treat audio as essential to quality, not optional polish
principles.why: Masterpieces exist with bad graphics or even without coherent game essence, but Sakurai can't name a single one with bad audio design.
principles.how: Give music and sound effects the same priority, schedule and attention as graphics.
principles.anti_pattern: Taking audio lightly.
principles.quote: And yet, I can't think of a single example of a masterpiece with bad audio design.

principles.principle: Build audio that players will remember first
principles.why: When people recall a game they loved, the music and sound effects are often the first things that come to mind; audio hits you right in the heart.
principles.how: Benchmark your music and sound effects against what you remember from games you loved, and construct even simple effects with care.
principles.example: Old games with only simple noise-based sound effects that still had well-constructed audio.
principles.quote: Even more than the game itself, its visuals, or its characters— audio is what hits you right in the heart.

summary: A director creates and also trims, cutting excess and steering the project back on course when plans slip, and that only works if team members report accurate information, including trouble, as early as possible.
takeaways: Directors trim excess, not just create
Course corrections are faster when the director leads them
Report trouble early with accurate information
Build teams where the baton passes quickly

principles.principle: As director, trim the excess yourself when plans slip
principles.why: It's faster when the director recognizes and addresses problems than when compromises come from producer-versus-director battles; finished products are the result of trimming and hard work.
principles.how: When hardware limits, deadlines or workload go off plan, anticipate the damage, cut or offload the riskiest work, and reset the course.
principles.anti_pattern: Leaving cuts to a fight between cost-focused producers and quality-focused directors.
principles.example: Offloading "the heavy or flammable cargo" to get back on course.
principles.quote: That's because a director not only creates, but is also responsible for trimming the excess.

principles.principle: Report trouble early with accurate information, even when struggling
principles.why: Decisions built on incorrect premises are all wrong, and someone who admits at the last minute they can't finish loses the time an earlier fix could have saved.
principles.how: Make it a rule to flag being stuck as soon as it happens, well before the deadline, with an honest status.
principles.anti_pattern: Struggling silently and saying you can't do it at the deadline.
principles.quote: And always give accurate information, even if you're having trouble!

principles.principle: Build cooperative relationships so work can be handed off quickly
principles.why: If a struggling member comes to the director during the process, an appropriate solution can likely be found before time is lost.
principles.how: Treat early reports as baton passes: reassign, re-scope or change approach right away.
principles.quote: Within a team, it's best to build a cooperative relationship where you can quickly pass the baton.

summary: Lead the way Sakurai remembers Satoru Iwata leading: trust creators with their content, step in personally when problems arise, meet trouble with calm logic instead of temper, and invest in direct, one-on-one communication.
takeaways: Trust creators with content; help when problems arise
Buggy code can't be fixed by tuning parameters
Stay calm and analytical where others lose their temper
Value one-on-one communication with your people
Names carry nuance: "Brothers" meant friends settling a disagreement

principles.principle: Trust creators with content, but step in when problems arise
principles.why: Iwata never told Sakurai how to approach his games' content, yet jumped in personally to help teams whenever problems came up.
principles.how: Let directors own creative decisions; when a team is stuck, get hands-on to fix the issue rather than dictating content.
principles.example: Iwata at HAL Laboratory, and later debugging Melee as head of Nintendo's corporate planning division.
principles.quote: Personally speaking, he never told me how I should approach the content of my games.

principles.principle: Fix bugs in the code before trying to tune parameters
principles.why: Even with correct parameters, mistakes in the code mean almost no adjustment gives the result you want, which wasted Sakurai's time as the one tuning.
principles.how: When tuning stops responding as expected, have programmers hunt the underlying bugs directly.
principles.anti_pattern: Tuning parameters on top of buggy code.
principles.example: Super Smash Bros. Melee's final stretch, when Iwata worked with the programmers to find the code problems.
principles.quote: Even if the parameters are set correctly, if the code itself has mistakes in it, almost no amount of adjustments can make things turn out how you want.

principles.principle: Meet problems with calm analysis instead of anger
principles.why: Iwata used logic rather than instinct, and where most people would lose their temper he stayed calm and offered analysis or suggestions.
principles.how: When something goes wrong, analyze the cause and propose a fix before reacting emotionally.
principles.anti_pattern: Losing your temper or taking offense.
principles.quote: In situations where most people would lose their temper or get offended, he would remain calm and offer analysis or suggestions instead.

principles.principle: Make time for one-on-one conversations with team members
principles.why: Iwata valued communication and found one-on-ones with employees incredibly effective, and wrote his own invitations despite his workload.
principles.how: Schedule regular one-on-ones and send important invitations personally rather than through an assistant.
principles.example: Iwata's one-on-ones from his HAL presidency onward.
principles.quote: he'd make time to talk with his employees one-on-one— something I believe he felt to be incredibly effective.

summary: A leader isn't above the team: a director's instructions flow downstream, but they are really requests made from the bottom up to the people doing the work, so treat everyone with respect and as an ally.
takeaways: Leaders make requests from the bottom up
Nobody on the team is higher or lower
Nobody likes a demanding customer; show respect
Teammates are allies even when you disagree

principles.principle: Treat directions to your team as requests, not orders
principles.why: People with ideas are powerless without others; instructions travel downstream, but the director is really asking the people who do the work, just as a publisher can't make customers buy.
principles.how: Phrase direction as requests to the people doing the work, and never bark orders.
principles.anti_pattern: Barking orders because you're the director or producer.
principles.example: Customer and publisher: the customer is downstream in distribution but upstream in choosing the game.
principles.quote: But in actuality, they're making requests from the bottom up to the dev team members who'll be doing the actual work.

principles.principle: Show every teammate respect regardless of rank or seniority
principles.why: Nobody likes a demanding customer, so acting superior breeds resentment; everyone on the team is an ally working toward a better product.
principles.how: Address all team members politely in name and tone, including new hires much younger than you, and treat disagreements as normal between allies.
principles.anti_pattern: Acting superior or subservient; addressing new coworkers casually.
principles.quote: Neither the director nor their team members should act superior or subservient to anyone else, I'd say.

summary: When you take on a big creative project next to your main job, plan and script all of it up front, prove it with a pilot, favor speed and brevity over perfection, clear reviews the day they arrive, and remember that shared knowledge only has meaning when people use it.
takeaways: Plan all content up front when juggling two big projects
Test feasibility with a finished pilot first
Short and snappy: speed above all else
Clear reviews the same day; set delivery cutoffs
Knowledge only has meaning when people use it

principles.principle: Plan and script the entire project before production starts
principles.why: Running the channel alongside a large game was only feasible if all content was decided in advance, and fixed categories also kept every material organized.
principles.how: Brainstorm one-line topics, group them into categories with fixed counts, cut weak ones, outline and write everything, then lay out releases in a spreadsheet that doubles as the tracker.
principles.anti_pattern: Improvising content as you go while juggling another big project.
principles.example: All 256 planned episode scripts were written before recording began.
principles.quote: In order to increase my chances of success, I absolutely had to plan all the content in advance.

principles.principle: Prove feasibility with a finished-quality pilot before committing
principles.why: Sakurai made a three-episode pilot to find out whether he could really make the channel, then used it to win Nintendo's cooperation and convince his editing company.
principles.how: Complete two or three representative pieces at final quality, use them as a go/no-go test, and show them to partners and rights holders.
principles.example: Pilot episodes C03 "Keeping Rewards in Sight," C11 "Praise the Player!" and D03 "Jump Physics."
principles.quote: I did this to find out whether or not I could really make this channel, and the answer was: Yes! I can do it!

principles.principle: Favor speed and brevity over perfecting every detail
principles.why: With limited time, over-working each script to prevent every misunderstanding would have cost succinctness; he calls this the secret to a good presentation.
principles.how: Write in fast passes (he averaged about 12 scripts a day) and accept living with the results.
principles.anti_pattern: Ruminating over every last detail.
principles.quote: Short and snappy! Speed above all else! And I'd have to live with the results.

principles.principle: Clear every review the same day, with a delivery cutoff
principles.why: Putting reviews off invites trouble, and late-night deliveries around 11 PM were wrecking his sleep.
principles.how: Require collaborators to deliver anything for same-day review by a fixed time (his was 8 PM), and send feedback as bullet points.
principles.anti_pattern: Letting review requests spill into the next day.
principles.example: HIKE's video and thumbnail deliveries, each episode getting about six to eight rounds of feedback.
principles.quote: Putting them off is just asking for trouble.
